edges.description: Bacteria from the infected sinus enter the orbit through thin bones, dehiscences, or venous channels and seed orbital fat, extraocular muscle, or subperiosteal spaces.
Inflammatory necrosis can consolidate into a pus collection inside the tight orbital compartment.
Postseptal inflammation causes diffuse periocular and lid edema.
Acute orbital inflammation can erythematously involve the eyelids.
Bacterial orbital infection can trigger a systemic febrile inflammatory response.
Abscess and edema increase orbital volume inside the tight bony orbit, producing raised intraorbital pressure.
Postseptal infection can extend through the superior ophthalmic venous drainage into the cavernous sinus and cause septic cavernous-sinus thrombosis.
Inflammatory volume expansion within the orbit pushes the globe forward.
Orbital congestion and raised pressure produce conjunctival edema.
Edema and pressure impair extraocular muscle excursion.
Restricted and misaligned ocular movement produces double vision.
Inflamed postseptal tissues and extraocular muscles cause pain when the eye moves.
Elevated pressure in the bony orbit compresses the optic nerve and its vascular supply.
Compression, thrombophlebitis, or ischemia injure the optic nerve during complicated orbital infection.
Optic neuritis, vascular occlusion, and compressive ischemia can produce visual loss.
Septic posterior spread can involve the meninges.
Septic posterior spread can seed intracranial abscesses.

nodes.description: Drainage of orbital or subperiosteal pus and ventilation of infected sinuses are surgical options when imaging or the clinical course shows a large abscess, intracranial extension, visual compromise, or failure of initial antibiotics.

evidence.snippet: The principles of surgical management are drainage of any pus and establishment of ventilation to the sinus.

evidence.reference_title: Management of pediatric orbital cellulitis: A systematic review.
evidence.snippet: Pre-septal and post-septal cellulitis can generally be managed non-surgically, while orbital abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis are managed surgically.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that cases requiring surgical management for SRC should undergo coinitial orbitotomy with FESS to reduce re-operation rates.

nodes.description: Systemic corticosteroids have been tested as adjuncts after initial antibiotic response to reduce orbital inflammation, but systematic-review evidence remains conflicting and they are not standard first-line therapy.

evidence.reference_title: Role of oral corticosteroids in orbital cellulitis.
evidence.snippet: Use of oral steroids as an adjunct to intravenous antibiotic therapy for orbital cellulitis may hasten resolution of inflammation with a low risk of exacerbating infection.

evidence.reference_title: Adjunctive systemic corticosteroids in pediatric orbital cellulitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
evidence.snippet: Adjunctive corticosteroids were not associated with shorter hospitalization and may be associated with increased risks of adverse outcomes.

Loss of vision can occur due to orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, optic neuritis, central retinal artery occlusion, and exposure keratopathy, and possible systemic sequelae include meningitis, intracranial abscess, osteomyelitis, and death.

nodes.description: Orbital infection can spread posteriorly through ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus, causing septic thrombosis and enabling extension to the meninges or brain.

evidence.snippet: The cardinal signs of orbital cellulitis include diffuse lid edema with or without erythema, conjunctival chemosis, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia.
Other ophthalmic signs may include mechanical ptosis, diplopia, raised retrobulbar resistance, globe dystopia, and/or deterioration of vision.
Orbital cellulitis can be distinguished clinically from preseptal cellulitis by its clinical presentation, such as conjunctival chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, pain with eye movements, and proptosis.
The cardinal signs of orbital cellulitis include diffuse lid edema with or without erythema, conjunctival chemosis, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia.
Patients may also present with systemic features like fever, malaise, associated nasal discharge, and cough.

nodes.description: Hospital admission with intravenous antibiotics is first-line therapy for orbital cellulitis, with empiric regimens chosen to cover Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and sometimes anaerobic organisms until cultures identify a narrower target.

evidence.snippet: There has been a generally widely accepted practice of using a broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage for Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms as the empirical first-line therapy at presentation, even before any culture sensitivity of the organisms is available.

evidence.reference_title: Microbiology and Epidemiology of Orbital Cellulitis in Pediatric and Young Adult Patients.
evidence.snippet: Empiric antibiotic selection should include an anti-methicillin-resistant S. aureus agent combined with a broad-spectrum beta-lactam and anaerobic coverage.

evidence.reference_title: Epidemiology and Management of Orbital Cellulitis in Children.
evidence.snippet: On HD 0, ampicillin/sulbactam was the most commonly prescribed regimen (175/220, 79.5%), followed by clindamycin (33/220, 15.0%) and ceftriaxone/vancomycin/metronidazole (28/220, 12.7%).

evidence.reference_title: Epidemiology and Management of Orbital Cellulitis in Children.
evidence.snippet: In a large cohort of children with orbital cellulitis over an 11-year period, we found that nearly all (95.9%) experienced resolution of disease within 30 days of completing antibiotic therapy.
